# Prescriptive lessons -- benson x method-vol-3-technique-arpeggios

## maj7

Benson treats maj7 chords -- specifically Cmaj7 as Imaj7 -- as the primary site of avoid-note discipline: the perfect 4th is proscribed by default but has contextual exceptions the player must judge. Melodic content over Imaj7 must combine arpeggio structures with scale lines (scales alone are insufficient), and the Cmaj7 chord shape doubles as a fretboard navigation anchor in the five-zone system. Pattern exercises are permitted as scaffolding only and must be offset with rhythmic displacement to avoid mechanical predictability.

- [ch.7 p.269] Descending "Major 7th Scale Arpeggios" -- Cmaj7 arpeggios with added color tones transcribed from Benson solos -- are prescribed zone by zone to create melodies fitting Ionian or Lydian contexts while sidestepping the perfect 4th avoid note. Each zone yields a guide idea from highest to lowest note.
- [ch.6 p.244; ch.7 p.269] The perfect 4th is an avoid note over Cmaj7 (Imaj7) and must not be used as a default melodic choice, because it "can create some melodic problems, especially over the root chord and the relative minor chord." Exceptions exist when the musical situation permits.
- [ch.6 p.244] Benson explicitly carves out the exception: "there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation." Player judgment governs; the proscription is a default, not an absolute.
- [ch.7 p.275] To produce a Lydian sound over Cmaj7, Benson prescribes superimposing a Gmaj7 arpeggio (G, B, D, F#), giving a C Lydian melody. On guitar this must be arpeggiated in sequence -- simultaneous voicing as on piano is not available.
- [ch.7 p.269] Scales alone are insufficient over Cmaj7: "it is not enough to only use the scales of the chords to create melodies, we must add stronger melodic structures to them such as triads and tetrads." Arpeggio structures are required reinforcement.
- [ch.4 p.141] The major blues scale is prescribed as playable over any individual major chord including maj7: the catch is it "can sound not bluesy," so the prescribed technique is to mix it with the minor blues scale in the same key to reach a blues vibe.
- [ch.6 p.246] The Cmaj7 chord shape is prescribed as the navigational anchor for Ionian-side zones in the five-zone fretboard system. Chord roots guide positional memory better than single notes; the shape is a navigational tool, not a harmonic instruction.
- [ch.7 p.275] Ascending Cmaj7 arpeggios define a single fretboard zone; descending Cmaj7 arpeggios with added notes span two zones because they are played vertically. Ascending forms orient position; descending forms are the primary melodic vehicle over Imaj7.
- [ch.7 p.270] Intervallic pattern exercises over Cmaj7 are scaffolding only -- "DO NOT rely on these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring." Every pattern must be applied with rhythmic displacement to become musical.
- [ch.7 p.269] For Fmaj7 (Lydian) within the C harmonic field, the natural major scale including the perfect 4th works freely. The avoid-note prohibition is specific to Imaj7 and VIm7, not all maj7 instances -- the curator should confirm this distinction is maintained in masters.json.

## min7

Benson's min7 teaching centers on two paired avoid-note rules -- the flat 6th over Am7/Aeolian parallels the perfect 4th over Cmaj7 -- and on the relationship between the minor pentatonic scale and the min7 chord identity. The five-zone fretboard system uses Am7 shapes as navigational anchors for relative-minor zones; minor pentatonic lines are preferred (not required) over minor chord family contexts but are explicitly permitted over maj7 and dom7 as well. Minor blues substitution tricks are prescribed for memorization before theory is understood.

- [ch.7 p.269] Descending "Minor 7th Scale Arpeggios" -- Am7 arpeggios with added color tones from Benson solos -- are prescribed zone by zone to create melodies fitting Dorian or Aeolian contexts while avoiding the flat 6th. Each zone yields a guide idea from highest to lowest note.
- [ch.6 p.244] The flat 6th is an avoid note over Am7 (VIm7/Aeolian): "Be careful with the avoid notes of both scales (perfect 4th in the Ionian mode, and flat 6th in the Aeolian mode), because they can clash with the melody note." Contextual exceptions apply.
- [ch.6 p.244] Exception: "there are always exceptions and at times the avoid note works fine depending on the situation." The flat-6th proscription over Am7 is a default, not a law; player judgment determines use.
- [ch.5 p.210] For min7 chords in the minor chord family, Benson's preference is to use unmixed minor pentatonic lick lines: "our preference is to use the lines over minor chords or chord sequences belonging to the minor chord family." This is a tendency, not a rule.
- [ch.5 p.210] Clarification and counter-example: unmixed minor pentatonic lines "will often work perfectly over major chords such as C6, Cmaj7 and of course C7." The minor-family preference does not restrict application -- these lines travel freely to dom7 and maj7 contexts.
- [ch.7 p.269] For Dm7 (Dorian) within the C harmonic field, the natural major scale including the perfect 4th avoid note works without restriction. The avoid-note proscription is specific to Imaj7 and VIm7 -- the curator should confirm Dorian min7 is not conflated with Aeolian min7 in masters.json.
- [ch.6 p.246] The Am7 chord shape is prescribed as the navigational anchor for Aeolian-side fretboard zones. "We visualize vertically but play horizontally most of the time" -- the shape is a positional memory tool, not a harmonic prescription.
- [ch.3 p.108] The minor pentatonic scale implies a min7 chord identity (A, C, E, G = Am7), and C6 and Am7 share the same notes ("C6 is an inverted Am7"). Despite this equivalence, the five-zone system requires visualizing them separately -- "it is extremely important to visualize them separately."
- [ch.5 p.195] Minor blues substitution tricks for min7 chords must be memorized before their theory is understood: "it is not necessary to understand the theory behind it, just memorize them." The minor blues form mixes minor and dominant chord types that pentatonic lines alone do not cleanly summarize.
- [ch.7 p.275] Ascending Am7 arpeggios define a single fretboard zone; descending Am7 arpeggios with added notes span two zones. The descending form is the primary melodic vehicle over VIm7.
- [ch.7 p.270] Intervallic pattern exercises over Am7 are scaffolding only: "DO NOT rely on these. They are exercises and can begin to sound very predictable and extremely boring." Rhythmic displacement is required to make any intervallic pattern musical.

## dom7

Benson treats dominant 7th chords in blues contexts as the primary site of scale-mixing discipline: no single blues scale may be used lazily across all changes, and the minor and major blues scales must be deployed chord by chord. The minor blues scale's major 3rd requires special velocity treatment, and the same-key mixing rule breaks down entirely in minor blues form. A separate note confirms that the natural major scale's perfect 4th avoid note is tolerated (not banned) over G7/Mixolydian within the harmonic field.

- [ch.4 p.151] For dominant 7th chords in a blues context, Benson prescribes combining minor and major blues scales chord by chord: "when we mix the major blues scale with the minor blues scale, we cannot summarize all the chords into one scale anymore, we must follow the harmony." The combination works for each dominant 7th chord individually.
- [ch.4 p.141] When applying the minor blues scale over a dominant 7th chord, the major 3rd must be played quickly within the phrase: "Make sure to play the major 3rd quickly in the phrase, otherwise the melody can sound wrong." This is a specific execution rule, not a harmonic one.
- [ch.4 p.141] The major blues scale is prescribed over any dominant 7th chord, but alone "can sound not bluesy" -- the prescribed fix is mixing it with the minor blues scale in the same key to recover blues vibe.
- [ch.4 p.140] Single-scale reliance over all dom7 changes is explicitly proscribed: "Be careful not to rely on this technique. It will make you sound like a lazy improviser. Your lines will lack variation and will sound stagnant." Overreliance on the blues scale is named as the failure mode.
- [ch.4 p.151] The same-key minor+major blues combination rule does not apply in minor blues form: "This will not work for minor blues form." In minor tonality, the C minor blues scale pairs with the Eb major blues scale, not the C major blues scale.
- [ch.5 p.210] Unmixed minor pentatonic lick lines also work over dominant 7th chords (C7 is cited explicitly) without mixture from the major pentatonic. This complements -- not contradicts -- the blues-scale prescription; the minor pentatonic is an additional permitted option.
- [ch.7 p.269] For G7 (Mixolydian) within the C harmonic field, the natural major scale works "perfectly... even while using the avoid note." The perfect 4th avoid note that is proscribed over Imaj7 is tolerated -- with care -- over the V7 chord.

## min7b5

Benson's only direct prescription for min7b5 concerns its position in the harmonic field: the Locrian chord (Bm7b5 in C major) tolerates the perfect 4th avoid note from the natural major scale without restriction. No separate melodic vocabulary or arpeggio system is specified for this chord quality in the extracted material.

- [ch.7 p.269] For Bm7b5 (Locrian) within the C harmonic field, the natural major scale including the perfect 4th avoid note works freely: "This scale works perfectly when played over... Locrian, even while using the avoid note. We must be careful with our note choices." The avoid-note proscription does not extend to Locrian.
